name: Yoncalla
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.note: Extinct Kalapuyan variety; only Mithun 1999 classification notes and Jacobs-era text collections; no Yoncalla phonology located

new_statements.quote: Frachtenberg occasionally does not mark stress, but he is remarkably consistent when he does show it. It occurs on both short and long vowels, and is thus independent of length [...]. In Mary's River, it falls on the first syllable of a stem; in Tualatin and Yoncalla, stress is often shifted to prefixed elements. If a prefix is added in Mary's River, stress does not move: wau·tso?, kuwau·tso?. Stress is accompanied generally by higher pitch (sometimes perhaps by lower pitch), which Jacobs calls "pitch accent." He says that pitch accent falls on "every syllable felt to be an independent root--nominal, pronominal, connective, or verbal" (1930: n.p.). Since stress is not always predictable from the segmental construction alone, it is considered to be phonemic.
new_statements.citation: Hajda, Yvonne P. 1976. Mary's River Kalapuyan: A Descriptive Phonology. MA thesis, Portland State University.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The family pattern (explicit for Mary's River / Central Kalapuya, and coded 'initial' by WALS from Berman 1990) is a pitch-accent/stress on the first syllable of the stem, unmoved by prefixation. For Yoncalla the only statement is a one-clause aside: stress is 'often shifted to prefixed elements', i.e. it does not stay on the stem-initial syllable but frequently lands on a prefix. No positional rule (initial, penultimate, etc.) is given for Yoncalla itself.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Yoncalla; 'often' implies the shift is not categorical.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (prefix+stem complexes), based on Frachtenberg's transcriptions and slip files; Hajda's own object is Mary's River, and the Yoncalla remark is comparative. Jacobs's 'pitch accent on every independent root' statement is family-general from an unpublished sketch.
new_statements.identity_note: Yoncalla = Southern Kalapuya (yonc1234, ISO sxk), distinct from Central Kalapuya (kala1400/kyl; Santiam, Mary's River) and Northern Kalapuya/Tualatin (tual1242/nrt). Hajda's Yoncalla data come via Frachtenberg's 1914 Grand Ronde notebook (Mrs Robert Allen, Mrs Tom Jackson) and slip files; Jacobs's 1928 Yonkalla data are from Laura Blackerty Albertson. The WALS 'Kalapuya' (klp) stress values are for Central Kalapuya, not Yoncalla.

sources.note: 'Suprasegmentals' p.45 (pdf p.53): stress independent of length; 'In Mary's River, it falls on the first syllable of a stem; in Tualatin and Yoncalla, stress is often shifted to prefixed elements'; quotes Jacobs 1930 ms that pitch accent falls on 'every syllable felt to be an independent root'; stress considered phonemic because not always predictable. The only published sentence on Yoncalla stress located.

sources.citation: WALS Online (Dryer & Haspelmath eds.), features 14A/15A/16A (Goedemans & van der Hulst) for 'Kalapuya' klp = Glottolog kala1400 (Central Kalapuya, ISO kyl), source Berman 1990.
sources.note: 14A Initial; 15A Fixed stress (no weight-sensitivity); 16A No weight -- second-hand from Berman 1990 and coded for Central Kalapuya, not Yoncalla.

sources.citation: Lewis, J. William. 2003. Central Kalapuya phonology: the segmental inventory of John Hudson's Santiam. MA thesis, University of Victoria. 319 pdf pp.
sources.note: Central Kalapuya (Santiam) only: accent 'always predictable as being on the left-most syllabic nucleus of the root' (p.3; p.63 fn.14); p.152 cites Jacobs ca.1930:46 that the pitch accent on the left-most root vowel rises about three notes. On Yoncalla: p.20 fn.23 'I am not familar with Yonkalla (SK) to comment on its prefixal system'; p.117 fn.53 discusses geminates in Jacobs nb45 Yonkalla data; App. V p.284 notes Laura Blackerty Albertson could give no texts. No Yoncalla stress statement.
